title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded for mirror-image molecule research
summary: Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on molecular chirality and asymmetric synthesis.
takeaways: Kagan's 1986 breakthrough: designing reactions to produce one chiral form over its mirror image
Soai created first chemical reaction producing only one mirror-image form (Soai reaction, demonstrated 2003)
Over half of clinically employed drugs are chiral molecules
Previously, chemists could only produce 'racemates' with equal mixtures of both mirror forms causing side effects or different therapeutic effects
Kagan (Université Paris-Sud, France) and Soai (Tokyo University of Science, Japan)
Prize citation: 'discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis'
Solves century-old puzzle of achieving homochirality synthetically
Kagan's 1986 key step; Soai's 1995 publication and 2003 demonstration of Soai reaction

The field originated from research on light-seeking algae and enables precise observation of what specia
takeaways: 2026 Nobel Prize recipients: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel
Optogenetics: uses light to control nerve cell activity
Originated from research on Chlamydomonas algae attracted to light
Hijacks ion channels to activate/deactivate neurons via light stimulation
Overcomes limitations of genetic deletion and physical brain damage methods
Allows activation and shutdown of neurons marked by individual gene activity
Three recipients: Deisseroth (Stanford), Hegemann (Humboldt), Nagel (Würzburg)
Optogenetics uses light to control individual neurons within milliseconds
Potential applications: blindness restoration, depression, Parkinson's, epilepsy, dementia
